tables.caption: Evaporation and condensation

original.text: Liquid water enters the air as water vapour during **evaporation**. When water vapour cools sufficiently, **condensation** forms tiny liquid droplets; clouds may contain droplets, ice crystals or both. Water can later fall as rain, flow over land or soak into the ground. Sunlight supplies energy for much of this cycling; water vapour itself is invisible.
original.correction: Make condensation explicit between evaporation and rain; do not represent visible cloud as vapour.

When water vapour cools sufficiently, **condensation** forms tiny liquid droplets; clouds may contain droplets, ice crystals or both.
revised.note: Water can later fall as rain, flow over land or soak into the ground. Sunlight supplies energy for much of this cycling; water vapour itself is invisible.

tables.caption: How early clocks mark time

items: **Sundial:** the shadow moves across a marked surface as the Sun’s apparent position changes. It needs sunlight and correct alignment.
**Water clock:** water drains from a marked vessel, or enters a floating bowl through a small hole until the bowl sinks. The device must be reset.
**Hourglass:** sand passes through a narrow opening between two bulbs. A particular amount of sand marks an interval.
**Candle clock:** a burning candle becomes shorter. Marks can indicate intervals, but draughts and uneven burning affect the result. Observe only an adult’s demonstration.

tables.caption: Resolution and accuracy

original.text: Timekeeping has improved greatly from early mechanical clocks to modern atomic standards. tables.caption: Different ways of obtaining food

items: **Bees and sunbirds:** take nectar from flowers using specialised mouthparts or a long tongue and beak.
**Young mammals:** obtain milk from their mothers. Humans, cows and many other mammals begin life this way.
**Pythons:** swallow prey whole, then digest it internally; swallowing whole does not mean skipping digestion.
**Filter-feeding aquatic animals:** collect small food particles carried in water. They do not obtain all their food by taking bites.

tables.caption: Contributions to digestion in the small intestine

items: **Liver:** makes bile, stored in the gallbladder. Bile disperses large fat globules into smaller droplets, giving enzymes more surface to work on. This physical dispersal is not the chemical digestion of fat.
**Pancreas:** supplies enzymes that act on carbohydrates, proteins and fats. Its bicarbonate-rich fluid helps neutralise the acidic mixture arriving from the stomach.
**Small-intestine lining:** supplies enzymes that help complete digestion, producing substances small enough to be absorbed.

tables.caption: Egestion and excretion

original.text: Material not absorbed in the small intestine moves into the large intestine, where more water and some salts are absorbed. Much water has already been absorbed in the small intestine. The remaining material forms stool, which is stored in the rectum and eventually passes out through the anus. **Egestion** removes undigested remains; **excretion** removes wastes produced by the body’s chemical processes.

tables.caption: Gas exchange in different animals

items: **Fish:** water passes over thin gill surfaces supplied with blood vessels. Oxygen dissolved in water enters the blood; carbon dioxide leaves. Fish do not split water molecules to obtain oxygen.
**Frogs:** tadpoles usually exchange gases through gills and skin. Adults use lungs and their moist skin; skin gas exchange can occur both in water and on land.
**Earthworms:** gases cross moist skin into and out of blood. Drying damages this exchange surface, so observe worms in place without handling or exposing them to dry air.
